questions.prompt: Phase I of the simplex method minimizes
questions.explanation: After the rows are written with a nonnegative right-hand side, each row receives an artificial variable and the auxiliary objective is the sum of those artificials. The original cost is set aside until a feasible basis is known. Minimizing the sum of the original variables is a different program. The right-hand side is data, not the objective.

questions.prompt: Phase I for \(x + 2y \ge 8\) and \(x + y \ge 3\), with \(x, y \ge 0\), starts from the artificial basis after the surpluses are introduced. What is the initial auxiliary objective?
questions.explanation: The equalities are \(x + 2y - s + a = 8\) and \(x + y - t + r = 3\). The artificial basis sets \(a = 8\) and \(r = 3\). The auxiliary objective is \(a + r = 11\). Reporting 8 or 3 reports one right-hand side. Reporting 5 reports a difference of those two numbers, which is not the objective.

questions.prompt: A positive optimal value of the auxiliary problem means
questions.explanation: Every feasible point of the original system gives the artificials the value zero, so the auxiliary optimum is zero whenever the original system is nonempty. A positive auxiliary optimum says no such point exists. It does not say the original objective is unbounded: unboundedness is a question about a nonempty feasible set. Restarting with the same constraints and a new auxiliary cost does not create a feasible point that the first auxiliary problem has already ruled out.

questions.prompt: Put these steps in the order used to build and read a phase-I problem.
questions.explanation: The sign of the right-hand side is fixed first, so that the artificial basis \(a = b\) is nonnegative. The auxiliary objective is then defined, and the simplex method starts from that artificial basis. The two readings of the optimum come after the method stops: a positive value is infeasibility, and a zero value is a feasible basis of the original system. Reading the optimum before the pivots uses the starting sum, which can be positive even when a later basis drives the artificials to zero.

steps: Put the constraints in equality form and make every right-hand side nonnegative.
Add one artificial variable to each equality and minimize the sum of the artificial variables, setting the original costs aside.
Run the simplex method from the basis consisting of the artificial variables.
If the auxiliary optimum is positive, declare the original program infeasible.
If the auxiliary optimum is zero, drop the artificial variables and keep the resulting basic feasible solution.

questions.prompt: At the artificial basis for \(x + 2y - s + a = 8\) and \(x + y - t + r = 3\), minimizing \(a + r\), which statements hold?
questions.explanation:
The artificial basis is \(a = 8\), \(r = 3\), and the objective is 11. With both artificial costs equal to 1, the reduced cost of a structural column is the negative of its column sum. The column of \(x\) sums to 2 and the column of \(y\) sums to 3, so the reduced costs are \(-2\) and \(-3\). Either may enter.
• A positive starting value does not prove infeasibility. The auxiliary problem may still reach 0.

The auxiliary objective equals 11.
\(x\) may enter, because its reduced cost is \(-2\).

\(y\) has reduced cost \(-3\).

questions.prompt: Both artificial variables are basic, each with cost 1, and an original column has entries \(a\) and \(b\). The phase-I reduced cost of that column is
questions.explanation: The original column has cost 0 in phase I. The basic cost is \((1, 1)\), and the basis is the identity, so the reduced cost is \(0 - (a + b) = -a - b\). On the declared ranges this is negative, which is why a column with a positive sum can enter. Using \(a + b\) forgets the minus and would say the auxiliary objective rises. Using \(-a\) drops the second row.

questions.prompt: A note runs phase I on \(x + y \le 12\) and \(x + y \ge 19\), with \(x, y \ge 0\). Exactly one step is false.
questions.explanation: One artificial is enough on the lower bound once the upper bound has its own slack. The gap between 19 and 12 is 7, and the auxiliary minimum is 7. A positive minimum means the original system is empty. The false step draws the opposite conclusion from that 7. The last step is the right reading of the same number.

steps: The auxiliary objective is the artificial variable, and the original costs are ignored.
An optimal auxiliary solution has artificial value 7.
The original pair of inequalities is therefore feasible.
A positive auxiliary optimum means no point satisfies both original inequalities.
reasons: An auxiliary optimum of 7 is positive, so the original system is empty.
The auxiliary objective should have included the original costs.
The artificial value 7 means the artificial variable is zero.

questions.prompt: For \(x + y \le 12\) and \(x + y \ge 19\), with \(x, y \ge 0\), what is the optimal value of the phase-I problem?
questions.explanation: Write \(x + y + s = 12\) and \(x + y - t + a = 19\). Subtracting gives \(a = s + t + 7\). Every nonnegative \(s\) and \(t\) makes \(a \ge 7\), and \(a = 7\) is attained at \(x = 12\), \(s = 0\), \(t = 0\). The original system would need \(a = 0\), which is impossible. Reporting 19 gives the starting artificial value. Reporting 12 gives the upper bound. Reporting 0 would mean the original system is feasible.

questions.prompt: An auxiliary optimal value of exactly zero means
questions.explanation: Zero is the best the artificial sum can be, and it is attained, so the artificials are zero at that basic solution. Dropping them leaves a basic feasible solution of the original equalities. It says nothing about the original objective: that objective is restored only after feasibility is known. A second copy of the artificials would change the system. Some original variables may still be zero; a basic solution often has zeros.

phase I must add a second copy of every artificial variable
the original system has a feasible solution, and the current basic point gives one
every original variable is positive

questions.prompt: In phase I for \(x + 2y - s + a = 8\) and \(x + y - t + r = 3\), the most negative reduced cost at the artificial basis belongs to \(y\). What step does the ratio test give?
questions.explanation: The column of \(y\) is \((2, 1)\), and the artificial values are 8 and 3. The ratios are \(8/2 = 4\) and \(3/1 = 3\). The step is 3, and \(r\) leaves. The new artificial value is \(8 - 2 \cdot 3 = 2\), with \(y = 3\). Reporting 4 uses the other ratio and would drive \(r\) negative. Reporting 8 or 2 reports an artificial value, not the step.

questions.prompt: Continue that phase-I problem until the auxiliary objective is optimal. In the basic feasible solution that is recovered, what is \(y\)?
questions.explanation: After the first pivot the basis is \(a = 2\), \(y = 3\), and the surplus \(t\) has reduced cost \(-2\). The ratio test gives step 1 and \(a\) leaves. The auxiliary value falls from 2 to 0. The resulting point has \(y = 4\), \(t = 1\), and every artificial equal to zero. Check: \(2 \cdot 4 = 8\) and \(4 - 1 = 3\). Reporting 3 stops at the first pivot. Reporting 2 reports the artificial value there. Reporting 0 reports an artificial variable rather than \(y\).

questions.prompt: During phase I, the original objective is
questions.explanation: Phase I answers a feasibility question. Its cost is the artificial sum, and the original coefficients are not part of that cost. Mixing the two costs can drive an artificial variable positive in exchange for a better original value, which does not produce a feasible point. The ratio test uses basic values and column entries, not the original cost. The original cost is allowed to have either sign; phase I does not need it.
questions.figure_alt: A straight line sloping downward on labeled axes.
options: added to the artificial sum so that every pivot improves both
ignored, and restored only after a feasible basis of the original system is known
used to break ties in the ratio test
required to be nonnegative before any artificial variable is added
